rationale: AC-002 (verifyValidator) and AC-003 (verifyDeposit) share the same root cause — missing access control on beacon-proof submission functions in CompoundingValidatorManager — and the same fix (add onlyRegistratorOrGovernor modifier). Both allow any caller to submit valid EIP-4788 Merkle proofs to mutate validator/deposit accounting state without authorization, and both impact lastVerifiedEthBalance / depositList accounting. The vulnerable functions differ (verifyValidator vs verifyDeposit), the specific state transitions differ, and the exploit paths are independently exercisable, so they should be submitted as separate findings. However, the root cause (no access control on permissionless proof-submission functions in the same contract) and the fix (same modifier on both functions) are materially identical, making this a high duplicate-risk pair within the batch.
recommendation: Submit both AC-002 and AC-003 as separate findings since the vulnerable functions and exploit paths differ, but explicitly cross-reference each other. The compound impact (both functions unguarded simultaneously) should be noted in each report. Do not merge into a single finding.

rationale.details: AC-003 and AC-002 share the same root cause category (missing access control modifier on an external function in CompoundingValidatorManager.sol) and the same fix template (add onlyRegistratorOrGovernor). However, the vulnerable functions differ — AC-002 targets verifyValidator() (lines 606-680) while AC-003 targets verifyDeposit() (lines 719-831). The exploit paths are distinct: AC-002 exploits mismatched withdrawal credentials to set validator state to INVALID and reduce lastVerifiedEthBalance, while AC-003 exploits the snapTimestamp==0 window to prematurely remove a deposit from depositList causing totalDepositsWei underreporting. The broken invariants differ: AC-002 breaks validator state integrity, AC-003 breaks deposit accounting timing. Both are independently exploitable. The duplicate risk is medium rather than high because the vulnerable functions, exploit paths, and broken invariants are distinct enough to warrant separate reports — the shared root cause category (missing modifier) and fix pattern are the only true overlaps. Each should be submitted separately with a cross-reference noting the compound accounting impact.
